subtitle: Journal-club style ICU update: PICO, key results, appraisal, bedside impact, and medical English.

script.heading: Intro
sentences: Welcome to Critical Care Daily for September 11, 2026.
Today we will review 3 recent ICU-relevant publications.
The format is quick listen first, then PICO, key results, critical appraisal, bedside impact, and medical English notes.
Use this as a morning triage tool, then open the source link for full-text appraisal before changing practice.

script.heading: Story 1 - Predictors of Critical Illness During Different COVID-19 Pande
sentences: Story 1 is about Predictors of Critical Illness During Different COVID-19 Pandemic Periods Compared With Seasonal Influenza..
This is a recent research article from Critical care medicine.

The clinical question is best framed as follows: in patients hospitalized for influenza between 2018 and 2022, how should we interpret Exposure or intervention stated in the title/objective. compared with Comparator or control group stated in the methods/results, if present.?
Age distributions varied across pandemic periods, with the Omicron period showing an age profile similar to influenza (≈ 50% ≥ 75 yr).

Adjusted hazard ratios for ICU-admission were strongest in unvaccinated patients, males, and individuals of 45-74 years for COVID-19, and in individuals of 45-64 years or with chronic lung diseases for influenza.
We included 92,428 COVID-19 hospitalizations and 21,355 influenza hospitalizations.
For critical appraisal, focus on whether the design supports a causal conclusion and whether the patients resemble your ICU population.

script.heading: Story 2 - Early renal perfusion phenotypes and renal recovery in critica
sentences: Story 2 is about Early renal perfusion phenotypes and renal recovery in critically ill patients with or at risk for acute kidney injury: a prospective multicenter cohort study..
This is a cohort study from Shock (Augusta, Ga.).

The clinical question is best framed as follows: in Critically ill adults with or at risk for AKI were enrolled within 24 h of intensive care unit admission in a prospective multicenter cohort from six ICUs in China, how should we interpret Exposure or intervention stated in the title/objective. compared with Comparator or control group stated in the methods/results, if present.?
Among 456 patients, 216 (47.4%) had AKI at ICU admission and 253 (55.5%) met AKI criteria within 72 h.
Two SQP phenotypes were identified: sustained-high perfusion (n = 224, 49.1%) and sustained-low perfusion (n = 232, 50.9%).

Sustained-high SQP was associated with lower odds of persistent AKI in the primary model (adjusted odds ratio, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.35-0.89; P = 0.015), although this association was attenuated in expanded sensitivity models.
For critical appraisal, focus on whether the design supports a causal conclusion and whether the patients resemble your ICU population.
The bedside implication is this: Use as background evidence; look for confounding and whether the exposure is modifiable at the bedside.

This is a cohort study from Shock (Augusta, Ga.).

The clinical question is best framed as follows: in patients with community-acquired sepsis admitted to the ICU within 6 h of ED presentation between September 2019 and December 2023, how should we interpret Exposure or intervention stated in the title/objective. compared with Comparator or control group stated in the methods/results, if present.?

In the validation cohort, ΔpH values below these thresholds consistently predicted higher 28-day mortality, with adjusted hazard ratios (HRs): overall (HR, 2.80; 95% confidence intervals (CI), 2.13-3.69; C = 0.678), acidosis (HR, 2.71; 95% CI, 1.66-4.43), normal (HR, 4.43; 95% CI, 2.81-7.00), and alkalosis (HR, 1.90; 95% CI, 1.04-3.48).
ΔpH showed a nonlinear association with mortality, with greater absolute deviations, particularly negative ΔpH linked to increased risk.
The optimal cutoffs differed by baseline status (-0.012 for acidosis, -0.145 for normal, and -0.240 for alkalosis).

script.heading: Outro
sentences: That wraps up today's journal club style update.
Before applying any finding, check the full source, the absolute effect size, and your local ICU context.
For English practice, repeat one academic phrase from each article out loud.

articles.title: Early renal perfusion phenotypes and renal recovery in critically ill patients with or at risk for acute kidney injury: a prospective multicenter cohort study.
articles.summary: Critically ill adults with or at risk for AKI were enrolled within 24 h of intensive care unit admission in a prospective multicenter cohort from six ICUs in China. Among 456 patients, 216 (47.4%) had AKI at ICU admission and 253 (55.5%) met AKI criteria within 72 h. Two SQP phenotypes were identified: sustained-high perfusion (n = 224, 49.1%) and sustained-low perfusion (n = 232, 50.9%). Sustained-high SQP was associated with lower odds of persistent AKI in the primary model (adjusted odds ratio, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.35-0.89; P = 0.015), although this association was attenuated in expanded sensitivity models. Sustained-high SQP was also associated with less renal non-recovery within 7 days, faster recovery among patients with AKI at admission, and less RRT use on day 3 and day 7.

articles.title: Early Arterial pH Changes as Strong Predictors of Mortality in Sepsis: A Multicenter Cohort Study.
articles.summary: This multicenter retrospective cohort study included 3,512 patients with community-acquired sepsis admitted to the ICU within 6 h of ED presentation between September 2019 and December 2023. Prognostic cutoffs were derived in a derivation cohort (70%) and validated in an independent cohort (30%). ΔpH showed a nonlinear association with mortality, with greater absolute deviations, particularly negative ΔpH linked to increased risk. In the validation cohort, ΔpH values below these thresholds consistently predicted higher 28-day mortality, with adjusted hazard ratios (HRs): overall (HR, 2.80; 95% confidence intervals (CI), 2.13-3.69; C = 0.678), acidosis (HR, 2.71; 95% CI, 1.66-4.43), normal (HR, 4.43; 95% CI, 2.81-7.00), and alkalosis (HR, 1.90; 95% CI, 1.04-3.48). To evaluate the prognostic significance of early arterial pH changes (ΔpH) during the transition from the emergency department (ED) to the intensive care unit (ICU) in patients with sepsis. The patients were stratified by baseline pH into acidosis (<7.35), normal (7.35-7.45), and alkalosis (>7.45). ΔpH was defined as the difference between ED pH and the lowest ICU pH within 24 h after ICU admission.
